stops.title: The question
stops.text: So far we have seen quantization for language models. Q-Diffusion asks whether the same post-training tricks work on diffusion models, with no retraining at all. The answer is no, at least not out of the box. A diffusion model runs one network many times, on inputs that change from pure noise to a clean image. It was the first to keep quality high with four bit weights, and it even works with eight bit activations, W four A eight. For this project, it is the origin of the calibration recipe used in NNCF.

stops.title: Two fixes, one picture
stops.text: Here is the whole paper in one diagram. On top, the gold bars show how wide the network's input is at each denoising step: wide while the sample is still noise, narrow near the final image. Naive quantization calibrates on one step and gets the wrong range for all the others. Q-Diffusion samples calibration data from every few steps across the whole trajectory. At the bottom, a skip connection glues together a large deep tensor and a small shallow one, so Q-Diffusion gives each half its own scale.

stops.title: Why diffusion is hard
stops.text: Now, why is this harder than quantizing a classifier? A classifier runs once. A diffusion sampler feeds the quantized network its own slightly wrong output, again and again, for every step. So a small rounding error at the start is carried into the next step and grows. A sampler with a hundred steps behaves like a network a hundred times deeper. On top of that, the activation ranges drift from step to step, so no single calibration snapshot represents them.

stops.title: Fix one: calibrate across time
stops.text: That is the problem. Here is the first fix. Run the full-precision model from random noise, and at every c-th step keep a batch of the real intermediate inputs. This gives a calibration set that covers the whole trajectory, with no training data needed. Then the paper uses a standard recipe called BRECQ: go block by block, and learn how to round each weight so the block's output matches full precision. Activation step sizes are learned afterwards, in the same block order.

stops.title: Fix two: split the shortcut
stops.text: The second fix is about the U-Net's skip connections. The decoder concatenates deep features, with values up to about forty, with shallow encoder features close to zero. One four bit scale sized for the big half rounds the small half to nothing. Notice the trick in this drawing. A convolution over concatenated channels is just the sum of two smaller products. So each half gets its own activation and weight quantizer, and the output is the same, with no extra compute.

stops.title: Which fix matters when
stops.text: This ablation separates the two fixes on CIFAR-10. With four bit weights only, calibration alone does most of the work: the FID falls from about 141 to 6.58, and splitting brings it to 5.09. Once activations are also eight bit, calibration alone stops at about 54. Splitting is what brings it down to 4.93, next to full precision at 4.22. So calibration handles time, and splitting becomes essential as soon as activations are quantized.

stops.title: Does it work?
stops.text: And here is the headline across three benchmarks, all at W four A eight. On CIFAR-10, linear quantization reaches an FID of about 188 and SQuant about 456, while Q-Diffusion gets 4.93. The bedroom and church models show the same pattern, staying within about 2.3 FID of full precision. One caveat: these are small U-Nets and Stable Diffusion, not transformers. And if the sampler changes without recalibrating, quality drops, especially with quantized activations.

stops.title: What the thesis takes from it
stops.text: So what goes into the thesis? The calibration recipe, directly. When building the NNCF dataset for LTX-2.3, hook the transformer's inputs during full pipeline runs and keep samples from many steps, including both guidance branches. Weight-only int8 or int4 barely depends on this, but W eight A eight does. Shortcut splitting does not apply to a transformer, but the lesson does: tensors that mix different ranges need separate scales or higher precision. Next, PTQ4DiT carries these ideas over to diffusion transformers.
